extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and philosophers of mathematics (researchers and advanced students)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for understanding, constructing, and judging mathematical proofs, including the roles of informal/creative moves, formal derivations, probabilistic algorithms, and community verification in establishing reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic-specific constructive moves ('Let...', 'Consider...')
rubrics_metrics.description: Such topic-specific moves are neither theorems nor results of applying rules of logic; they are habitually introduced with imperatives like 'Let...' or 'Consider...' and are standard in mathematical discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These moves are creative, intentional steps that construct conceptual 'bridges' between given data or intermediate steps and later parts of the argument. They have no independent logical justification other than serving the purpose of the proof (examples: Euclid's consideration of P1P2...pn + 1; introducing cosets in Lagrange's theorem). They are transferable 'technologies' to other proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating properties of constructed objects
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient merely to write down a constructed object; one must show that it has the required properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: writing the Hellegouarch–Frey elliptic curve is not enough — one must show it is semistable and non-modular. Achieving this can require intricate intermediate constructions and links and may demand collaboration of experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal consistency of axioms (skyscraper grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalised mathematical theories would possess 'skyscraper grounding' provided that the underlying axioms are consistent; hence proving consistency of axioms is paramount for such grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Hilbert's Problem Number 2 and rests on Hilbert's Thesis (every mathematical proof can be converted into a formal derivation). The text warns that skyscraper grounding is unattainable in practice and that Hilbert's Thesis is an article of faith with known difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic cohesiveness (component testing and certification)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative model ('spaceship' model) views mathematical knowledge as an assemblage of individually manufactured and tested components whose coherent functioning yields reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs should be built from constituents whose reliability has been previously tested (certified components). Typical practice: establish claims (components), 'put them on the shelf' as certified, then assemble them in a clinching argument. This emphasizes tested tools, reuse, and the cumulative character of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical components guarantee coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical components of proofs are the 'nuts and bolts' that hold together the conceptual framework produced by methodological components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical structure preserves the coherence of the whole mathematical system and allows outcomes of new proofs to be added as warranted assertions; logical parts ensure systemic cohesiveness even when methodological parts generate innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological components generate innovations and links
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological elements of proofs (constructions, strategies) generate conceptual innovations, establish contextual links, and serve as problem-solving methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These aspects are often neglected relative to formal derivations, yet they are central to how proofs create and systematise mathematical knowledge and how techniques transfer across problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning assimilation and explanatory detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductions in proofs depend on an understanding and prior assimilation of the meanings of the concepts involved; mere formal definitions without explanation impede comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, providing definitions on the board without detailed explanation blocks understanding even at graduate level. There is also a difficulty in specifying how consensus is reached on correct meaning-dependent inferences in informal deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between formal derivations and informal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal derivations belong to the formal/syntactic realm; proofs as practiced are informal, meaning-dependent, and cannot be defined technically in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should not conflate derivations and proofs. Even when symbol manipulation is central, most proofs differ substantially from formal derivations. The assumption (Hilbert's Thesis) that every informal proof can be fully formalised is questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of probabilistic algorithms and Monte‑Carlo tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilistic algorithms (e.g., Rabin's primality test) are constructed and validated by rigorous mathematics and are tools whose probabilistic statements concern the algorithm's reliability, not the truth of mathematical statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret 'algorithm declares prime with high probability' as 'the integer is probably prime' — the integer is either prime or not. For applications like cryptography, a trade-off between computational ease and a small error margin is appropriate; such technical results have no direct epistemological license to relax proof standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability limits of probabilistic checking / transparent proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilistic (spot-checking) methods and 'transparent' or holographic proofs allow verification of formal derivations with high confidence via a small number of checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods operate on fully formalised, syntactic objects. Applying them to mainstream informal proofs would require complete, often massive formalisation (definitions, notation, axiom schemes, etc.), raising practical and epistemological obstacles. Thus PCP-style results do not obviate the informal, semantic practices of mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social processes and collective verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is a collective enterprise; cross-checking, criticism, and independent verification by the community are primary mechanisms for detecting and correcting errors and for establishing reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The social process enhances objectivity and reliability; mathematicians' errors are corrected socially rather than solely by formal symbolic logic. Community 'immune system' will detect defective 'grafts' in the literature over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against assigning probabilistic truth‑values to theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal to assign numerical probabilities to the 'truth' or 'proof value' of theorems (the 'probabilist' view) is impractical and incoherent in realistic dependent proof trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracing conditional probabilities through chains of probabilistically proven theorems is intractable; recursive dependence and uncertain probabilities for background results make a meaningful numerical truth-assignment unworkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and certification of background 'machinery' (storehouse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs rely on background certified machinery (standard tools like bijections, induction, arithmetic tools) drawn from a community storehouse of proven results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When establishing intermediate claims, one should isolate logical parts from technical parts, justify claims, and then reuse them as 'certified' components. Proper use requires justification of those background tools as reliable components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits of full formalisation and machine verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Completely formalising a significant mathematical proof (and the surrounding background) to feed into a computer verifier entails enormous, often unrealistic appendices (definitions, axioms, inference rules, implementations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if formalisation were in principle possible, questions remain: who will carry out and certify the formalisation, and how feasible is the task? Probabilistic machine verdicts also compute algorithm error probabilities distinct from the correctness of the mathematical claim, so machine checks do not straightforwardly replace human mathematical practice.
